terms.gloss: strain, the straining of the mind
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.21, against relaxātiō (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. stress: nimia vīrium contentiō (Egger)
terms.comment: Contentiō is a stretching, an exertion of body or mind; Cicero sets it against relaxātiō and remissiō, rest. Too much of it is stress: Egger’s nimia vīrium contentiō. Its other common senses are a contest or dispute, and a comparison. Stressed is sollicitus (worried) or occupātissimus (swamped); stressful, molestus or labōriōsus.
Where the stress is worry (see concern).

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.18: angor est aegritūdō premēns; 4.27 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Properly a choking; a passing feeling, where anxietās is a lasting state (Cic. Tusc. 4.27).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 12.30.2: maximīs occupātiōnibus distinēbar (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: For the stress of having too much to do.

phrases.latin: sed dīcēs mē ipsum mihi sollicitūdinem struere.
phrases.english: but you will say I am making stress for myself.

phrases.latin: remōtum ā sollicitūdinibus et cūrīs et necessitāte cotīdiē aliquid contrā animum faciendī
phrases.english: far from worries and cares and the need to do something against one’s inclination every day

phrases.latin: omnemque vītae suae cursum in labōre corporis atque in animī contentiōne cōnficeret
phrases.english: and spent his whole life in physical toil and mental strain
